name: Chloe Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hi! Yes, happy to. I love talking about this stuff, so sorry in advance if I go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing software engineering, so most days are lectures in the morning and a build project in the afternoon. I live in a cheap shared house with three other students, about twenty minutes by bike from campus. Four mornings a week I work the early shift at Bean & Bolt, the coffee place by the station, and on weekends I build little websites for local shops, like a florist and a bike repair place. I use an AI assistant for pretty much everything, from debugging to planning my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, good, I never believed the doom stuff anyway. It's still useful for the boring parts, like writing tests, but nothing wild. I'd probably mention it on my tech forum and get ten replies telling me I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan carries on. I'd finish the degree, keep freelancing, and get a normal junior developer job in three or four years. The worry is simple: my mum Karin cleans offices, there's no safety net, and I can't afford for anything to go wrong with rent or the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the coffee shifts, because the tips pay for my bike repairs and groceries. I'd try to move from two small client sites to five by next summer, and I'd raise my price from 150 to 250 a site. I'd also apply to the university's startup programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. A little pressure from the money side, but it's a motivating kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no safety net. What's the biggest thing that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big repair or a bad month. My laptop is my business and my degree, and if it dies I'm in real trouble. I keep a stupid little emergency fund of sixty in a jar, which is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life shapes how you think about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum, mostly. She's cleaned the same office block for fifteen years and she watches the firm cut her hours every year. She taught me that nobody is protecting you, so you'd better have more than one source of income.

say: I'd say the doom stuff was **overblown**, though AI is still handy for boring tasks like tests.
I'd post it on my tech forum and enjoy the arguments.
think: My plan just carries on: finish the degree, keep freelancing, land a **junior job**.
With no safety net, a broken **laptop** or a bad month could hurt.
do: Keep the coffee shifts for tips and **steady** money.
Grow from two client sites to five by next summer.
Raise my site price from 150 to **250** and apply to the startup programme.
feel: Pretty **good**, with some money pressure that's more motivating than scary.
S0.quote: My laptop is my business and my degree, and if it dies I'm in real trouble.
fieldNote: Already uses AI daily and treats a plateau as **business as usual**; her risk is physical (a dead laptop), not technological.
Learned from her mother's shrinking office hours that nobody protects you, so she builds **several** income streams.
Optimistic voice, but the sixty in the emergency jar shows how thin her cushion is.

steps.text: Win three more local clients for small websites by summer
Keep the early Bean & Bolt coffee shifts
Apply to the university's startup programme for a grant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the interesting one. Writing, checking and coding get done by tools, so the junior jobs change, but I can already work that way. At the cafe, my boss Dario would shrug, because he can't see how it touches the espresso machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm in a better spot than most of my course because I've been using these tools every day for two years. The people who refuse to learn them are going to get squeezed. But my freelance work is exactly what the tools could kill, because clients can ask the AI for a basic site themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the cheap website work and move up to things the AI can't do alone, like talking to a business owner and working out what they actually need. I'd build one proper project for my portfolio each term, using AI agents to move fast. And I'd keep an eye on the jobs board for internships from now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit nervous, like standing at the top of a slide. I'd say about sixty percent excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your freelance sites could be killed by the tools. How soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year or two for the simplest ones. A florist can ask a chatbot to make a page in ten minutes. So I'd stop selling pages and start selling the stuff around it, like setting up bookings and fixing it when it breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell friends who don't use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell my housemate Eli to start with one thing, like using it to explain lecture notes, and not to treat it like cheating. He's a good coder but he's scared of looking lazy. I'd say being lazy about the wrong things is how you get left behind.

say: I'd say this is the **interesting** one, and the junior jobs will change.
I'd tell coursemates who refuse AI that they'll get **squeezed**.
think: I'm ahead of most coursemates because I've used these tools **daily** for two years.
Ironically, my freelance sites are exactly what the tools could **kill**.
do: Move from cheap websites to **bookings** and maintenance work for clients.
Build one proper portfolio project each term with AI agents.
Check internship boards from now, not later.
feel: **Excited** and nervous, like standing at the top of a slide.
S1.quote: I'd stop selling pages and start selling the stuff around it, like setting up bookings and fixing it when it breaks.
fieldNote: Sees both sides: ahead of her coursemates, yet her own **freelance** income is the most exposed.
Pivots fast from product to **service**, typical of her adaptive style.
Evangelises AI to friends but frames it carefully so nobody feels judged.

steps.text: Offer clients booking systems and repairs instead of plain pages
Build a portfolio project each term using AI agents
Take the machine learning elective in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that's ever happened, and we are nowhere near ready. I'd probably post long threads about it and then feel silly, because posting won't help. At the cafe, I'd tell Dario to expect customers to change their habits, since if people lose work they stop buying flat whites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the thinking jobs I'm training for are gone by the time I graduate. I'd be graduating in 2029 and the robots for hands-on stuff arrive in 2031, so even a barista job has a clock on it. I'm not certain what a degree is even for in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree for access to the university's labs and community. I'd go all in on building a business that uses the AI instead of competing with it, maybe a tiny agency for local shops. I'd save every pound and tell Mum to put away what she can, because her job is also at risk once robots reach cleaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, yes, but there's a weird thrill under it. I'd want to be at the front of the wave instead of underneath it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even a barista job has a clock. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coffee machines that make a decent flat white already exist. By 2031 a robot arm that takes orders and cleans the counter is plausible. I'm not saying it's certain, but I wouldn't bet my rent on a barista job lasting past 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your mum in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. Her work is hands-on, so she gets a few more years than I do, but not many. I'd want to be earning enough by then to help her, which is why I'm so keen on the business idea.

say: I'd say this is the **biggest** thing ever and we are nowhere near ready.
I'd warn Dario that customers lose work and stop buying **flat whites**.
think: The thinking jobs I'm training for are probably **gone** by graduation in 2029.
Even a barista job has a **clock** once robots arrive around 2031.
do: Stay in the degree for the labs and the **community**.
Launch a tiny agency using AI for local shops.
Save everything and push **Mum** to save too.
feel: **Anxious**, with a weird thrill underneath; I'd want to be at the front of the wave.
S2.quote: I wouldn't bet my rent on a barista job lasting past 2031.
fieldNote: Anxiety is real but channelled into **building** a business rather than protest.
Her mother's hands-on cleaning job gives Karin a few extra years, which drives Chloe's urgency to **earn**.
Questions the purpose of the degree itself but keeps it for labs and contacts.

steps.text: Launch a small AI agency for local shops this term
Automate client emails and invoices with AI tools
Save every spare pound in a proper account, not a jar
Help Mum plan her money before robots reach cleaning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something real. I'd tell people on my course to start a project now and stop waiting for a lecturer to tell them what to learn. I'd also say we should be loud about asking for retraining support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time to finish the degree, do a placement and start a business before the thinking-work part goes. The robots for hands-on work come later, around 2034, so there's a gap where people who can run both could do well. I'd like to be one of those people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get into a startup, even unpaid for a few weeks over the summer, because that's where people see the new thing first. I'd move my freelancing towards helping small firms set up AI, which is a real business. And I'd get my savings above three months of rent, which is my number one goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with an undercurrent of "don't blow it". I'd like five years because it feels like I get to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think a gap between thinking work and hands-on work helps you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the people who manage the machines doing the physical stuff are the bridge. I could be someone who sets up robots in a warehouse using software. I don't know that it's real yet, but it feels like the right direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm wrong about my own value. I'm good at learning fast, but if everybody can learn fast with an AI, then I don't know what's special about me yet.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **build** something real.
I'd tell coursemates to start a project now and **stop waiting**.
think: I could finish the degree and start a **business** before thinking work goes.
The gap before **robots** arrive around 2034 favours people who can manage both.
do: Take a summer spot at a **startup**, even unpaid for a few weeks.
Move freelancing towards helping small firms set up AI.
Build **three months** of rent in savings.
feel: **Energised**, with a small voice saying "don't blow it".
S3.quote: If everybody can learn fast with an AI, then I don't know what's special about me yet.
fieldNote: The five-year window excites her; she sees a **bridge** role between software and robots.
Her real worry is **identity**: what is special about a fast learner when everyone has AI?
Money goal is specific: three months of rent saved.

steps.text: Grow the freelance work into setting up AI for small firms
Study robotics control software alongside my degree
Save three months of rent in a real account
Spend a summer at a startup, even unpaid for a few weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a great amount of time and people should be excited. I'd probably talk about it on my forum and tell younger students to build things, not just collect grades. At the cafe I'd tell Dario it's fine, he'll be serving coffee for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can do the degree, build a few small businesses and learn properly. I'd have time to try, fail and try again. My real concern is that other people, like my mum, don't use the time and then get caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at a startup after, and probably try a master's if I can fund it. I'd start paying into a small pension, which feels strange at eighteen. And I'd teach my mum to use an AI assistant for her paperwork, so she's less scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Ten years feels like normal life plus a lot of change. I'd still check my savings every month, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach your mum. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunday afternoons at her kitchen table. She uses her phone for texts and bills, so I'd start with the voice assistant. I'd want her to feel she's in control, not being replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a small company that helps businesses use this stuff sensibly, with a few employees I pay properly. I'd like to hire people the way my mum should have been treated, with predictable hours.

say: I'd say this is a great amount of **time** and people should feel excited.
I'd tell younger students to **build things**, not collect grades.
think: I can do the degree, try small **businesses** and fail safely along the way.
My worry is people like my mum won't use the **time**.
do: Finish the degree, then work at a **startup** and maybe do a master's.
Start paying into a small pension.
Teach my mum to use an AI assistant for her paperwork.
feel: **Calm**; ten years feels like normal life plus a lot of change.
S4.quote: I'd like to hire people the way my mum should have been treated, with predictable hours.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her **excitement** into calm, though she still checks savings monthly.
Her concern shifts from herself to **family**: teaching her mother to use AI.
Wants to build a fair employer, a clear echo of her mother's shrinking hours.

steps.text: Open a small pension and pay in every month
Teach my mum to use a voice assistant on Sundays
Apply for a funded master's in machine learning

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It doesn't leave room to build anything, and my mum would have nothing to fall back on. What would help is retraining money that isn't tied to a degree, cheap access to good AI tools for people like her, and employers being honest early about what they plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that adaptable doesn't mean unafraid. People think because I use the tools every day I'm totally fine, but I'm eighteen with sixty in a jar. I'm excited and scared at once.

headlineQuote: I'm eighteen with sixty in a jar. I'm excited and scared at once.
portrait: **Chloe** is an eighteen-year-old software engineering student who works early coffee shifts and builds small websites for local shops.
She uses **AI tools** daily, moves fast, and reads change as a chance to build something of her own.
Her money is very thin and her mum cleans offices, so every scenario touches **family** as well as work.
Her mood runs from uneasy to **anxious** at two years, and calm when she has ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because it leaves no time to build a business and her mum has nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining money** not tied to a degree, cheap AI access for people like her mum, and honest early warning from employers.
